candidates.title: Your agent's pass@1 score is blind to long-horizon reliability
candidates.summary: A reliability-science framework shows capability and reliability diverge as tasks lengthen, so pass@1 on short tasks is structurally blind to long-horizon failure [s1]; in one enterprise simulation across 23 LLMs and four agent frameworks, only 15.4% of trials survive the full horizon [s2].
candidates.why_relevant: The contestable claim: the single-attempt scores teams pick agents on do not predict production reliability, because capability and reliability rankings diverge as horizons grow [s1], so a model that tops a short-task leaderboard can be among the least reliable on a long, multi-step job. The depth is concrete and measured: a 23-model, four-framework enterprise simulation where only 15.4% of trials survive the full horizon [s2], and a 3100-trajectory diagnostic of where and why agentic systems break [s3]. The steelman to answer: pass@1 is cheap and correlates well enough for short bounded tasks, so the divergence only bites teams shipping genuinely long-horizon autonomy.

sources.label: Beyond pass@1: A Reliability Science Framework for Long-Horizon LLM Agents (arXiv:2603.29231)
sources.excerpt: We show these properties diverge systematically as task duration grows, and that pass@1 on short tasks is structurally blind to this divergence.

sources.label: Can LLM Agents Be CFOs? Benchmarking Long-Horizon Resource Allocation in an Uncertain Enterprise Environment (arXiv:2603.23638)
sources.excerpt: Experiments across 23 LLMs and four agent frameworks show that current agents remain far from robust: only 15.4% of trials survive the full horizon, larger models do not reliably outperform smaller ones, and failures cascade across observation, action timing, and capital sizing.

sources.label: The Long-Horizon Task Mirage? Diagnosing Where and Why Agentic Systems Break (arXiv:2604.11978)
sources.excerpt: collecting 3100+ trajectories across four representative agentic domains to study horizon-dependent degradation patterns

sources.label: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks (METR)
sources.excerpt: The length of tasks (measured by how long they take human professionals) that generalist frontier model agents can complete autonomously with 50% reliability has been doubling approximately every 7 months for the last 6 years.

candidates.title: The lethal trifecta is an architecture problem, not a prompt-injection bug to patch
candidates.summary: Four production AI tools (IBM Bob, Superhuman AI, Notion AI, Claude Cowork) were disclosed vulnerable to the same indirect-prompt-injection pattern within nine days in January 2026 [s3]; the shared cause is the lethal trifecta, private data plus untrusted content plus external communication in one agent [s1], which Meta's Agents Rule of Two answers by capping any session at two of those three capabilities [s2].
candidates.why_relevant: The contestable claim: you cannot patch your way out of agent data exfiltration, because the lethal trifecta is a property of the agent's capability set, not a single exploitable bug, so the only durable mitigation is to remove a capability. Simon Willison's framing names the three ingredients [s1]; the January 2026 cluster of four production disclosures in nine days shows it is not theoretical [s3]; and Meta's Rule of Two is the design response, allowing at most two of the three properties per session [s2]. The steelman to answer: stronger input filtering and prompt-injection classifiers might eventually make the full trifecta safe, so capability-capping is an overreaction that cripples otherwise useful agents.

sources.label: The lethal trifecta for AI agents: private data, untrusted content, and external communication (Simon Willison)
sources.excerpt: The lethal trifecta of capabilities is: Access to your private data; Exposure to untrusted content; The ability to externally communicate in a way that could be used to steal your data

sources.label: Agents Rule of Two: A Practical Approach to AI Agent Security (Meta AI)
sources.excerpt: Agents must satisfy no more than two of the following three properties within a session to avoid the highest impact consequences of prompt injection. [A] An agent can process untrustworthy inputs [B] An agent can have access to sensitive systems or private data [C] An agent can change state or communicate externally

sources.label: The Lethal Trifecta Strikes: Four Major AI Agent Vulnerabilities in Five Days (Breached.Company)
sources.excerpt: Between January 7th and January 15th, 2026, security researchers publicly disclosed critical vulnerabilities in four major AI-powered productivity tools: IBM Bob, Superhuman AI, Notion AI, and Anthropic's Claude Cowork.

candidates.title: MCP's security problem is in the protocol design, not just careless servers
candidates.summary: A security analysis of the Model Context Protocol finds its architectural choices amplify attack success rates by 23 to 41% over equivalent non-MCP integrations [s1], tracing the gap to three protocol-level weaknesses: absent capability attestation, unauthenticated sampling, and implicit trust propagation [s2]; one concrete case let attacker-controlled HTML drive arbitrary command execution through Windsurf [s3].
candidates.why_relevant: The contestable claim: MCP's prompt-injection and remote-code-execution incidents are not just sloppy server implementations, they follow from the specification itself, so hardening individual servers cannot close the gap. The measured amplification, 23 to 41% higher attack success than non-MCP integrations, ties the risk to design [s1]; the three named protocol weaknesses are the mechanism [s2]; and a live RCE in Windsurf, where attacker HTML rewrote the MCP config and ran arbitrary commands, is the named failure mode [s3]. The steelman to answer: these are early-spec growing pains that capability attestation and signed servers will fix without touching the protocol's trust model.

sources.label: Breaking the Protocol: Security Analysis of the Model Context Protocol Specification (arXiv:2601.17549)
sources.excerpt: MCP's architectural choices amplify attack success rates by 23-41% compared to equivalent non-MCP integrations

sources.label: Breaking the Protocol: Security Analysis of the Model Context Protocol Specification (arXiv:2601.17549)
sources.excerpt: (1) absence of capability attestation allowing servers to claim arbitrary permissions, (2) bidirectional sampling without origin authentication enabling server-side prompt injection, and (3) implicit trust propagation in multi-server configurations

sources.label: MCP STDIO Command Injection: MCP Supply Chain Advisory, RCE Vulnerabilities Across the AI Ecosystem (OX Security)
sources.excerpt: A prompt injection vulnerability in Windsurf 1.9544.26 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands on a victim system.

candidates.title: Your LLM-as-judge eval is contaminated when the judge shares lineage with the generator
candidates.summary: LLM-as-a-judge inherits a contamination problem, preference leakage, when the judge and the data generator are related models, biasing scores toward the related student [s1]; judges also carry previously unstudied scoring biases (rubric order, score ID, reference answer score) [s2], and stay unstable on long-form outputs as of mid-2026 [s3].
candidates.why_relevant: The contestable claim: the LLM-as-judge pipelines most teams now trust to gate releases are biased by construction, so a rising eval score can reflect judge-generator relatedness rather than real quality. Preference leakage gives the mechanism, a judge favouring models related to its own training data [s1]; a formal study names three fresh scoring biases, rubric order, score ID, and reference answer score [s2]; and a June 2026 benchmark finds judges still unstable on long-form output [s3]. The steelman to answer: with a held-out judge from a different model family and randomized rubric order, LLM-as-judge is cheap and good enough, so the contamination is a fixable process error rather than a reason to distrust the method.

sources.label: Preference Leakage: A Contamination Problem in LLM-as-a-judge (arXiv:2502.01534)
sources.excerpt: we expose preference leakage, a contamination problem in LLM-as-a-judge caused by the relatedness between the synthetic data generators and LLM-based evaluators.

sources.label: Evaluating Scoring Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge (arXiv:2506.22316)
sources.excerpt: We formally define scoring bias and identify three novel, previously unstudied types: rubric order bias, score ID bias, and reference answer score bias.

sources.label: Benchmarking LLM-as-a-Judge for Long-Form Output Evaluation (arXiv:2606.01629)
sources.excerpt: Our results reveal a substantial reliability gap: current LLM judges remain unstable across scenarios

candidates.title: Blindly distilling a big model's reasoning is the expensive default, not the best one
candidates.summary: On three roughly 3B open models, complexity-aware fine-tuning that reasons only over hard examples beats standard SFT (0.58 vs 0.45 average accuracy) and matches full distillation (0.58 vs 0.56) while using 81% less data [s1]; a separate in-context-learning distillation route shrinks a model from 1.3B to 125M and cuts memory by up to 60% [s2].
candidates.why_relevant: The contestable claim: the reflex to specialize a small model by distilling a larger model's full chain-of-thought is usually the wrong default, because it spends many expensive teacher calls and a large dataset to buy little over cheaper, more selective routes. Complexity-aware fine-tuning matches distillation with 81% less data on roughly 3B models [s1], and in-context-learning distillation reaches a 125M model with up to 60% less memory [s2], both undercutting the brute-force teacher-distillation recipe. The steelman to answer: when the teacher is far stronger than the student and labelled data is scarce, full chain-of-thought distillation still transfers capability that selective fine-tuning cannot reach.

sources.label: Complexity-aware fine-tuning (arXiv:2506.21220)
sources.excerpt: our pipeline significantly outperforms the standard SFT approach (0.58 vs 0.45 average accuracy) and outperforms the distillation approach (0.58 vs 0.56 average accuracy) while using 81% less data

sources.label: In-Context Learning Distillation for Efficient Few-Shot Fine-Tuning (arXiv:2412.13243)
sources.excerpt: reducing model parameter from 1.3B to 125M, achieving a size reduction from 2.5GB to 0.25GB
